surface_mechanism_description: The H2 pulse removes oxygen from the surface, transforming the film from iridium oxide to metallic Ir. The hydrogen pulse is not necessary for obtaining metallic films when O2 is used as a reactant, but removing the adsorbed oxygen before the next Ir(acac)3 pulse affects film growth and properties. The reaction mechanism involves the removal of oxygen by hydrogen, leading to a bare iridium surface which allows for faster surface diffusion and more effective crystal growth towards the (111) orientation.
evidence: In the O 2 process this adsorbed oxygen combusts some of the ligands during the Ir(acac)3 pulse, which reduces steric hindrance between the adsorbed metal precursor molecules and further increases their adsorption density and finally film growth rate. In previous ALD studies H2 has indeed been found to react with the surface oxygen releasing water at 195 °C in the Ir(acac)3+O3+H2 process 19 and at 200 °C in the Ru(EtCp)+O2+H2 process 22 . In ultra4high vacuum studies hydrogen has been observed to desorb from single crystal iridium surfaces mostly at 100 °C or below.28–32 This is also in accordance with the scheme recently proposed by Lu and Elam 22 for the Ru(EtCp)2+O2+H2 process at 150–200 °C, where the surface is assumed to be bare ruthenium after the H2 pulse. Knapas and Ritala 19 also concluded that in the Ir(acac)3+O3+H2 process the hydrogen does not remain on the surface, as no gaseous byproducts were formed during the following Ir(acac)3 pulse. This is in contrast to the Ir(acac)3+O2 process, where combustion occurs also during the Ir(acac)3 pulse due to the adsorbed oxygen layer. Thus it seems that H2 only serves to remove the adsorbed oxygen, in agreement with the observed decrease in the growth rate.
